questions.stem:
An architect joined a new firm three months ago after eight years at her previous firm, where she was project architect for an award-winning art museum. The new firm is preparing a proposal for a university museum, and the marketing coordinator wants to feature the art museum prominently. The previous firm was the architect of record.

How should the proposal present the art museum?

options.text: As a firm project, noting her role as project architect
options.explanation: The current firm didn't design the museum. Listing it as a firm project misrepresents the firm's experience.

options.text: Under her personal experience, naming the architect of record
options.explanation: Correct. Stating her actual role and crediting the firm of record is accurate (NCARB 3.3–3.4; AIA 4.201).

options.text: As a firm project, with written permission from the previous firm
options.explanation: Permission doesn't change who designed it. It would still misrepresent the current firm's experience.

options.text: It shouldn't appear in the proposal at all
options.explanation: Individuals may describe their own past experience, as long as they do it accurately.

questions.explanation: Claim credit accurately: your actual role, and the architect of record.

questions.stem:
During construction documents for a three-story office building, the owner directs the architect to delete the fire-rated corridor walls on the upper floors to save money. The architect explains in writing that the change violates the building code and would endanger occupants. The owner replies that the building official 'won't notice' and insists.

Under the NCARB Model Rules of Conduct, what must the architect do?

options.text: Revise the drawings and document the owner's direction in writing.
options.explanation: Documenting an unlawful direction doesn't permit the architect to design in violation of the code (NCARB 1.2).

options.text: Refuse to consent and report the decision to the building official.
options.explanation: Correct. NCARB Rule 3.5 requires refusing consent and reporting. If such decisions will continue, the architect terminates services unless the matter is resolved another way.

options.text: Obtain a written indemnification from the owner before revising.
options.explanation: An indemnity moves financial risk. It doesn't lift the duty to protect public safety.

options.text: Withdraw from the project immediately without further action.
options.explanation: Withdrawing alone skips the required refusal and report, and under Rule 3.5 termination is conditional.

questions.explanation: NCARB 3.5: refuse to consent → report to the building official → terminate if it continues. AIA 2.105 adds 'advise against' first.

questions.stem:
After a competitor was accused of copying another firm's house designs, a principal plans a lunch-and-learn on copyright. She wants to correct some common misunderstandings she has heard around the office.

Which statements about copyright in architectural work are correct under U.S. law?

options.text: Copyright protects a building's design, not just its drawings.
options.explanation: Correct. Architectural works are a protected category (17 U.S.C. §102(a)(8)).

options.text: Registration is required before suing over a U.S. work.
options.explanation: Correct. 17 U.S.C. §411(a) requires registration (or preregistration) before an infringement suit.

options.text: Protection begins when the design is registered.
options.explanation: Protection begins when the work is fixed in a tangible form. Registration affects enforcement, not protection.

options.text: Photographing a building from a public street is infringement.
options.explanation: Pictures of buildings visible from public places are expressly permitted (§120(a)).

options.text: Individual standard features, such as windows, are protected.
options.explanation: The definition of 'architectural work' excludes individual standard features (§101).

options.text: A client who pays the full fee owns the copyright under B101.
options.explanation: Under B101-2017 the architect keeps the copyright, and the owner receives a license.

questions.explanation: Know what's protected (designs, not standard features), when protection starts (on fixation), and what registration changes (the right to sue, remedies).

questions.stem:
A firm hires a freelance designer for a three-week assignment to develop a façade concept for a mixed-use project. The designer works from home on her own computer, invoices a flat fee, and delivers a concept the client loves. The firm and the designer never signed a written agreement.

Who most likely owns the copyright in the façade concept?

options.text: The firm, because it paid for the work
options.explanation: Payment alone doesn't transfer copyright from an independent contractor.

options.text: The freelance designer
options.explanation: Correct. Architectural works can't be commissioned works made for hire (17 U.S.C. §101), so the freelancer owns the concept unless she assigns it in writing.

options.text: The firm and the designer jointly
options.explanation: Joint authorship requires an intent to merge contributions into one work. Paying for a design doesn't create it.

options.text: The project owner
options.explanation: The owner has no claim to the freelancer's copyright without a written transfer.

questions.explanation: Get written copyright assignments from freelancers and consultants.

questions.stem:
A flooring manufacturer's sales representative tells an architect that the company will pay the firm a 3% commission on product sales for every project where the firm specifies its flooring. The representative notes that the product meets every performance requirement in the firm's current specification and costs less than competing products.

What should the architect do?

options.text: Decline the arrangement.
options.explanation: Correct. NCARB Rule 2.2 prohibits soliciting or accepting supplier compensation for specifying products, and it allows no waiver.

options.text: Accept it and disclose it to the client in writing.
options.explanation: Disclosure cures some conflicts, but not this one. Rule 2.2 has no waiver.

options.text: Accept it and credit the commission against the client's fee.
options.explanation: Crediting the money doesn't remove the influence on product selection. The arrangement is still prohibited.

options.text: Accept it only when the product is the best choice anyway.
options.explanation: Payment tied to specification compromises independent judgment, whatever the product's merit.

questions.explanation: Supplier compensation for specifying products is prohibited. Customary hospitality and product education aren't compensation.

questions.stem:
During a public interview for a new school, a competing architect tells the school board that your firm's last school 'failed its structural inspection and had to be shored.' The statement is false: the school passed every inspection. Two board members later repeat the claim to a reporter.

Which term best describes the competing architect's statement?

options.text: Libel
options.explanation: Libel is written or published defamation. The architect's statement was spoken.

options.text: Slander
options.explanation: Correct. A spoken false statement of fact that harms reputation is slander.

options.text: Plagiarism
options.explanation: Plagiarism is presenting another's work as your own.

options.text: Misrepresentation of qualifications
options.explanation: That refers to misstating one's own qualifications, not making false statements about a competitor.

questions.explanation: Defamation is a false statement of fact that harms reputation. Libel is written; slander is spoken.

questions.stem:
A firm is updating its ethics training after a staff member asked how the NCARB Model Rules of Conduct apply to everyday work. The trainer prepares four scenarios drawn from recent projects.

Which scenario describes conduct consistent with the Model Rules?

options.text: Sealing consultant drawings the architect reviewed and incorporated
options.explanation: Correct. NCARB Rule 5.2 lets the architect of record seal consultant information it has reviewed and incorporated into its own submissions.

options.text: Sealing a licensed consultant's drawings without reviewing them
options.explanation: Rule 5.2 requires review and a reasonable basis to trust the information before sealing it.

options.text: Accepting a supplier's paid trip for specifying its product
options.explanation: Benefits given in exchange for specifying products are prohibited compensation (Rule 2.2).

options.text: Voting on a commission matter involving the firm's own client
options.explanation: A financial interest in the matter is a conflict the architect must avoid (Rules 2.3, 2.6).

questions.explanation: Seal what you control or have reviewed, never trade specifications for benefits, and avoid acting where you have an interest.

questions.stem:
A licensed architect who has never joined the AIA advertises that her firm 'designed' a library she worked on as a junior employee at another firm. A competitor who is an AIA member files a complaint with the AIA's National Ethics Council and also contacts the state licensing board.

Which statement is correct?

options.text: The AIA can suspend her license to practice.
options.explanation: Only the state licensing board can discipline a license. The AIA acts only on membership.

options.text: The AIA Code doesn't apply, but the board's rules do.
options.explanation: Correct. The AIA Code binds only AIA members. Every licensee is bound by the jurisdiction's laws and rules, which typically prohibit misrepresenting credit.

options.text: NCARB will enforce the AIA Code for non-members.
options.explanation: NCARB doesn't enforce the AIA Code. It publishes model rules that boards adopt.

options.text: The AIA Code applies because she holds a license.
options.explanation: Licensure doesn't create AIA membership obligations.

questions.explanation: AIA Code = members only (membership sanctions). Board rules = all licensees (license discipline).

questions.stem:
A client shows an architect a house in another architect's online portfolio and asks for 'the same house with a few changes' on the client's lot. The client points out that the plans and photos are posted publicly, and offers to sign a statement accepting any legal risk.

What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Proceed, since the plans were posted publicly.
options.explanation: Posting a design publicly doesn't place it in the public domain.

options.text: Proceed if the design is substantially modified.
options.explanation: There's no safe-harbor percentage. A design substantially similar to protected expression can still infringe.

options.text: License the design, or create an original one.
options.explanation: Correct. Copying protected work needs permission. Otherwise, design something original that meets the client's goals.

options.text: Proceed if the client signs the risk statement.
options.explanation: A client's statement doesn't make infringement lawful. The architect would still be a direct infringer.

questions.explanation: Copying protected designs requires permission. Modifications and client assurances don't cure infringement.

questions.stem:
An architect has served on her city's planning commission for three years. Her firm has just been hired by a developer whose 200-unit project will come before the commission for site plan approval next month. She is confident she can review the project objectively, and the commission is short of members.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Disclose the conflict and recuse herself from the matter.
options.explanation: Correct. A public official with a financial interest in a matter must not participate in it (NCARB 2.3, 2.6; AIA 2.103).

options.text: Disclose the relationship and vote impartially.
options.explanation: Disclosure alone isn't enough when she would be judging her own firm's project.

options.text: Have another principal manage the project so she can vote.
options.explanation: The firm's financial interest is the same no matter who manages the project.

options.text: Resign from the commission before the hearing.
options.explanation: Recusal on this matter resolves the conflict. Resignation isn't required.

questions.stem:
Two firms submitted proposals for a public library. A complaint filed with the AIA's National Ethics Council compares them:

| Proposal element | Firm A | Firm B |
|---|---|---|
| Fee | $612,000 | $490,000 |
| Concept sketch | Not included | Included at no charge |
| Discount on a future second phase | None | 10% |

Firm A alleges that Firm B, whose principals are AIA members, acted unethically by undercutting the fee, offering free design work and promising a discount. What is the likely outcome under the 2024 AIA Code?

options.text: No violation for any of these practices
options.explanation: Correct. The Code's antitrust statement says competitive price quotations, discounts and free services are not, in themselves, unethical.

options.text: A violation for undercutting the competitor's fee
options.explanation: Price competition isn't a Code violation, and antitrust law bars the AIA from prohibiting it.

options.text: A violation for the free concept sketch
options.explanation: Free services aren't, in themselves, unethical under the Code.

options.text: A violation for the future-phase discount
options.explanation: Discounts aren't, in themselves, unethical under the Code.

questions.explanation: Competitive bids, discounts and free services are permitted under the AIA Code. Whether they're wise is a business decision.

flashcards.front: Who is bound by the AIA Code of Ethics?
flashcards.back: AIA members only. Sanctions affect membership, not licensure.
The state (jurisdictional) licensing board, under its law and rules of conduct.

flashcards.front: NCARB Model Rules of Conduct are…
flashcards.back: A model set of conduct rules (rev. July 2023) that boards adopt in whole or in part. Six rules: Competence, Conflict of Interest, Full Disclosure, Compliance with Laws, Signing & Sealing, AXP Supervisor obligations.
I General Obligations · II Public · III Client · IV Profession · V Colleagues · VI Environment

flashcards.front: Client overrules you on an unsafe code violation: model-rule response
flashcards.back: NCARB 3.5: refuse to consent → report to the building official → terminate services if it will continue (unless resolved otherwise). AIA 2.105 adds 'advise against the decision' first.

flashcards.front: Supplier offers a commission for specifying its product
flashcards.back: Decline. NCARB 2.2 prohibits supplier compensation for specifying or endorsing products, with no waiver. Customary hospitality and product education are OK.
Libel = written or published defamation. Slander = spoken. Both need a false statement of fact. Truth is a defense.
Plagiarism is an honesty issue: passing off others' work as yours. Infringement is a legal violation of exclusive rights. They can overlap.
When the work is fixed in tangible form. Registration isn't required for protection.
It's required before suing (U.S. works), and timely registration allows statutory damages and attorneys' fees.
Added buildings (overall form, arrangement of spaces and elements) as protected works; 17 U.S.C. §102(a)(8).

flashcards.front: Freelancer's design: who owns the copyright?
flashcards.back: The freelancer, unless there's a signed written assignment. Architectural works can't be 'commissioned works made for hire' (17 U.S.C. §101). Employees' work within scope belongs to the employer.

flashcards.front: Claiming credit for work done at a prior firm
flashcards.back: Allowed as personal experience if you state your actual role and credit the firm of record.
Sealing documents not prepared under your responsible control. Prohibited.

flashcards.front: Serving on a public board that reviews your firm's project
flashcards.back: Disclose the conflict and recuse yourself from that matter.
Admonition (confidential), censure, suspension of membership, termination of membership (made public).
Competitive bids or price quotes, discounts, and free services are not, in themselves, unethical.

flashcards.front: Duty to report another architect's violation
flashcards.back: NCARB 3.9: report violations of the jurisdiction's practice laws to the board. AIA 4.101: file a complaint with the National Ethics Council (serious violations).

flashcards.front: Conflict of interest: what cures it?
flashcards.back: Full disclosure and a written waiver by all parties (NCARB 2.3). AIA 3.201: consent of all who rely on your judgment after full disclosure.
